put two and two together.example: How slow he’d been, putting two and two together.
put two and two together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put up with.meaning: To accept something unpleasant without complaining.
put up with.example: So Charlie had to put up with their company as well.
put up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

raise his eyebrows.meaning: To lift your eyebrows to show surprise.
raise his eyebrows.example: Benjamin raised his eyebrows and looked at his dog.
raise his eyebrows.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

rather than.example: Rather than stand over her, they knelt on the ground behind Charlie.
rather than.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

run along.meaning: (1) To run beside or on something like a path ("They ran along the path"). (2) (Said to children) Go away now.
run along.example: You did a great deal, and now you must run along.
run along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

run off.meaning: To run away from a place.
run off.example: said Olivia, and she ran off in the direction of High Street.
run off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set off.example: Uncle Paton set off again at his usual breakneck speed.
set off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set out.meaning: To place things where people can see or use them.
set out.example: There were plenty of dishes full of delicious-looking food set out on the counter.
set out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake her head.meaning: To move your head from side to side to say "no".
shake her head.example: Onimous looked hard at her husband and vigorously shook her head.
shake her head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake his head.meaning: To move your head from side to side to say "no".
shake his head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shut up.example: Liv, shut up and listen,” said Fidelio.
shut up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

side by side.example: Charlie saw Dagbert and Gabriel heading for the door, side by side, deep in conversation.
side by side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sit down.meaning: To move your body onto a seat or the ground.
sit down.example: She sat down, happily sweeping her feathery tail back and forth across the ground.
sit down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sit up.meaning: To move from lying down to sitting.
sit up.example: She opened her eyes and sat up, clapping her hands.
sit up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

size up.meaning: To look at something carefully to judge it.
size up.example: Olivia took her time, sizing up the huge garment
size up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

slip away.meaning: To leave quietly, so that nobody notices.
slip away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

slow down.example: When Blessed approached the eerie region of the attics, Cook slowed down.
slow down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

so to speak.meaning: Used to say that your words are not exactly true but show the idea.
so to speak.example: now that Lyell has, so to speak, woken up.
so to speak.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sort of.example: It was the sort of place that made you speak very softly.
sort of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

speed up.example: As they speeded up, Charlie was thrown forward.
speed up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand her ground.meaning: To stay where you are and not give in (said of a woman or girl).
stand her ground.example: He felt even prouder when she stood her ground against a torrent of ridicule from Agnes Prout.
stand her ground.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand his ground.meaning: To stay where you are and not give in.
stand his ground.example: Weedon always made him uneasy, but today he stood his ground.
stand his ground.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand up.meaning: (1) To get onto your feet. (2) (Of hair or feathers) To point straight up ("His coarse hair was standing up like a hedgehog’s").
stand up.example: Charlie stood up, his eyes never leaving the trembling boy on the floor.
stand up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

step back.example: Charlie stepped back from the blank stare of the protruding stone eyes.
step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

straighten up.meaning: To stand straight again after bending.
straighten up.example: Maisie straightened up and took her bowl back to the sink.
straighten up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sweep away.meaning: (Of water or wind) To carry something away with great force.
sweep away.example: He drowned her parents, swept away her home, and murdered her fiancé.
sweep away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

swing around.example: Cook got to her feet and swung around.
swing around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

switch off.meaning: To stop a light or machine with a switch.
switch off.example: Matron switched off the light and marched out, slamming the door behind her.
switch off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often before doing something hard.
take a deep breath.example: She took a deep breath and imagined herself soaring up toward the stars.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a step back.example: Charlie took a step back from the window.
take a step back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care of.example: “I know someone who will take care of you,” he said.
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take her time.meaning: To do something slowly, without hurrying.
take her time.example: Olivia took her time, sizing up the huge garment
take her time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take no notice.meaning: To pay no attention to someone or something.
take no notice.example: When Charlie stood up, Dagbert took no notice.
take no notice.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take off.example: Mrs. Kettle took off her coat and told the boys to do the same.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take place.example: Drama lessons took place in the school theater.
take place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take up.meaning: (1) (Take up the call) To continue something that another person started. (2) "Take up positions" = go to the places where you will stay ("they took up their positions").
take up.example: Aries, the copper cat, took up the call, and then the yellow cat, Sagittarius, trilled a finale.
take up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

taken aback.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the worse for wear.meaning: Damaged, dirty or tired after a hard time.
the worse for wear.example: Joshua Tilpin looked very much the worse for wear.
the worse for wear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

there there.meaning: Kind words you say to calm someone who is sad or upset. It is not about a place.
there there.example: “There, there, dear. Charlie meant no harm, I’m sure.”
there there.usageNote: Informal. Said in a gentle, kind way.

track him down.example: they tracked him down in no time.
track him down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn away.meaning: To turn so that you are not facing someone.
turn away.example: Charlie called out to him, but he turned away and went through a door farther down the hallway.
turn away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn out.meaning: (1) To switch off a light. (2) To come to an event ("half the city turned out to watch"). (3) To become or develop in a certain way ("the way you’ve turned out").
turn out.example: Half the city had turned out to watch.
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn up.example: The people I live with won’t understand if I don’t turn up tonight.
turn up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

under her breath.meaning: Very quietly, so that others cannot hear.
under her breath.example: She wriggled out of his grasp, muttering under her breath, then rushed upstairs.
under her breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

used to.meaning: (1) Did something regularly in the past, but not now. (2) "Be used to" something = know it well so it does not seem strange ("she was used to unsafe places").
used to.example: We need to find the clothes Asa used to wear as a disguise
used to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wake up.example: He woke up to find someone shaking his shoulder.
wake up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

ward off.example: their combined efforts were enough to ward off the flames.
ward off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

well well.meaning: What you say when you are surprised to see someone or something.
well well.example: “Well, well, it’s you,” they heard her say.
well well.usageNote: Informal. People also say "Well, well, well."

what on earth.meaning: Said to show great surprise, like "what?".
what on earth.example: What on earth’s going on in Piminy Street?” said Olivia
what on earth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what's going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

who on earth.meaning: Said to show great surprise, like "who?".
who on earth.example: Who on earth would want to marry her?
who on earth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wide awake.example: At number twelve Filbert Street, Benjamin Brown was still wide awake.
wide awake.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

work out.meaning: (1) To do exercise. (2) To understand something by thinking. (3) To plan something ("it’s all worked out").
work out.example: Silly of me to try and work out here,” she said in a small voice.
work out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cross one's mind.meaning: To come into your thoughts for a moment.

in that case.example: “In that case, we must conclude that they are related.

in charge.meaning: Having the job of controlling something.
in charge.example: With no one in charge, it was difficult to apply themselves to work.

for goodness sake.meaning: Said when you are cross and want someone to stop or to listen.
for goodness sake.example: “For goodness’ sake, can’t you learn to control yourself, Tancred Torsson?” Dorcas grumbled as she bent to retrieve a book.

dog ahoy.meaning: A hello the bird shouts at a dog. Ahoy is a hello from a person on a ship.
dog ahoy.example: The sound of barking came from the café; this was followed by several catcalls, a low whinny, and a voice that kept repeating, “Dog ahoy!

blow me down.meaning: A surprised shout. It means I cannot believe this.
blow me down.example: Olivia had just begun to say, “But who …” when they heard Norton Cross open the café door and say, “Blow me down!”

chain mail.meaning: Metal clothes a fighter wears, made of many small rings.
chain mail.example: He donned a suit of chain mail and a helmet with a plume of red feathers.

give someone a ring.example: If you want to stop at the shop for lunch, give me a ring.”

back and forth.meaning: One way and then the other, again and again.
back and forth.example: “I know.” Olivia clicked her glittery shoes together and hopped back and forth.

lights out.meaning: The time at night when the lights must go off and students must not talk.
lights out.example: On Thursday night, only five minutes after lights-out, Dagbert decided to tell a bedtime story.

paragraphs.context: He is descended from Borlath, elder son of the Red King.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Manfred Bloor comes from the family of the cruel Borlath.
paragraphs.simple: This is from the list of endowed children. Manfred is a hypnotist: he can control people with his eyes. His power comes from Borlath, the Red King's cruel older son.

background.note: A magician-king who came out of Africa long ago. All the endowed children are descended from his ten children.
The Red King's eldest son, a cruel tyrant. Manfred is descended from him.
To put someone into a sleep-like state and control their mind. Manfred Bloor's endowment.

paragraphs.context: Naren can send shadow words over great distances.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Naren can send messages made of shadows.
paragraphs.simple: Naren is Bartholomew Bloor's adopted daughter. She can send "shadow words" far away. Her power comes from a grandson of the Red King who was taken to China by pirates.

background.note: Ezekiel's son, who has lived far away for many years. He returns with his adopted daughter Naren.
A girl from China, Bartholomew Bloor's adopted daughter. She is endowed: she can send 'shadow words'.

paragraphs.context: Charlie can travel into photographs and pictures.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie's power comes from both sides of his family.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie can go into pictures and photos by magic. His father's family comes from the Red King, and his mother's family comes from Mathonwy, a magician from Wales.

background.note: A Welsh magician from long ago, the Red King's good friend.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert is the son of Lord Grimwald, who can control the oceans.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert, the new boy, is a "drowner".
paragraphs.simple: Dagbert's father controls the sea. His mother made gold charms from the teeth of drowned men to keep Dagbert safe. Dagbert can drown people with his power.

background.note: A new boy at Bloor's who wears sea-gold charms. He is the son of Lord Grimwald and is a 'drowner'.
Dagbert's father, a powerful, frightening man who can control the oceans.
Someone who can drown people with water and waves. Dagbert's endowment.
Dagbert Endless's father, a cold, sea-smelling man who can control the oceans and the tides.

paragraphs.context: Billy can communicate with animals.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy can talk to animals.
paragraphs.simple: Billy's power comes from an ancestor who talked to ravens. The ravens sat on the gallows where criminals were hanged. People were afraid of him and made him leave his village.

background.note: A small white-haired orphan who lives at Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can talk to animals.

paragraphs.context: Her surname derives from the Spanish swordsman from Toledo
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma can turn into a bird, and her family links all the endowed.
paragraphs.simple: Emma's family name comes from a swordsman from Toledo in Spain. His daughter married the Red King, so he is an ancestor of all the endowed children.

background.note: A quiet art student with long blond hair. She is endowed: she can turn into a bird and fly.
The children at Bloor's with magic powers from the Red King. Here 'endowed' means 'born with a magic gift'.

paragraphs.context: The city began nine hundred years ago with a castle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The city's history begins with the Red King.
paragraphs.simple: The prologue tells the story of the city. The Red King built a castle 900 years ago. He wore a red cloak and had a burning sun on his shield. He was African and a magician.

background.note: The Red King's red cloak. It is very old and has magic power.

paragraphs.context: When the king’s beloved queen, Berenice, died, he went to grieve in the forest.
paragraphs.mainIdea: After his wife died, the king went away.
paragraphs.simple: When Queen Berenice died, the king went into the forest to be sad alone. He thought his ten children were safe, because they had good helpers and each child had a magic power.

background.note: The Red King's wife. When she died, five of their children turned wicked.

paragraphs.context: At that time, the country was a violent and lawless place
paragraphs.mainIdea: The king became a knight to help poor people.
paragraphs.simple: The country was dangerous: there was a lot of murder and robbery. So the king put on chain mail and a helmet with red feathers, made a magic sword and rode out to protect people.

paragraphs.context: For five years the Red King fought tyrants, murderers, and plundering nobles.
paragraphs.mainIdea: When the king came home, his children had gone bad.
paragraphs.simple: After five years of fighting, the king came back. Five of his children had left, and the other five were using their powers to do terrible things. The sad king left his castle forever.

paragraphs.context: Charlie’s grandmother and her three sisters all have a part in the evil.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie's bad relatives sent him to Bloor's Academy.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma Bone and her sisters are on the evil side. While Charlie's father was under a spell, they sent Charlie to Bloor's Academy. Charlie is often afraid there, but his endowed friends help him.

background.note: Lyell Bone, Charlie's father. For years he was under a spell and did not know who he was. At the end of book 5 he woke up and came home.

paragraphs.context: With his own talent for traveling into the past through pictures
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is learning the city's secrets.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie can go into the past through pictures, so he is learning old secrets. It is dangerous, but he has friends and he trusts the Red King.

paragraphs.context: This time, at least Charlie knew where his father had gone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie's parents go on holiday, but Charlie stays at home.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie's father is well again, and he takes Charlie's mother on a second honeymoon to watch whales and dolphins. Charlie chose to stay at home because he wants to solve some mysteries.

paragraphs.context: A stale, mildewy smell filled the hallway.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie and Uncle Paton look inside an old empty house.
paragraphs.simple: The house smells damp and old. The floor is dirty and the wallpaper is torn. Charlie looks into the room where he saw a light, but it is empty. Uncle Paton points to the kitchen.

background.note: Charlie's great-uncle, Grandma Bone's brother. He hides from daylight because his endowment makes lights burst. He helps Charlie.

paragraphs.context: A shuffling sound could be heard.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two strange figures run away from the house.
paragraphs.simple: They hear a noise. The kitchen is empty too, but the back door bangs open. Charlie sees two figures run through a broken fence at the end of the yard.

paragraphs.context: Paton Yewbeam, another of the Red King’s descendants, had inherited an unfortunate endowment.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton's power makes lights explode.
paragraphs.simple: If Uncle Paton looks at a light that is on, the bulb gets very hot and explodes. So he rarely goes out in the day. He is embarrassed by his strange power.

paragraphs.context: Uncle Paton’s four sisters were each as bad as the other.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton's four sisters are all horrible.
paragraphs.simple: The four sisters hate their brother because he does not agree with their bad ways. They are mean, unkind, proud, dishonest and greedy. None of them was ever kind to Charlie.

background.note: Charlie's grandmother, his father's mother. She was born a Yewbeam. She is cold and bossy and spies on Charlie.

paragraphs.context: Anything was better than spending the evening in the same house as Grandma Bone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie walks with Benjamin and a strange mist comes.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie goes to the park with Benjamin and Runner Bean. Benjamin always worries about his dog. Then a strange, salty mist starts to come into the street.

background.note: Charlie's best friend, who lives across Filbert Street. He is not endowed and goes to a different school.
Benjamin's big, friendly yellow dog. He often helps Charlie and his friends.

paragraphs.context: Father and son followed the burly figure down a long stone hall
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert and his father are taken through Bloor's Academy.
paragraphs.simple: A big man leads Lord Grimwald and Dagbert through the school, into the Music Tower, up a spiral staircase and along a carpeted corridor.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert will not disobey. If he does, he will die.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lord Grimwald explains the curse on his family.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Grimwald says that in his family, a son always turns against his father when he becomes powerful, and one of them dies. He and Dagbert have promised to work together.

paragraphs.context: So you know the story of the Red King?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ezekiel says the Flame cats hurt his grandson.
paragraphs.simple: Ezekiel tells Dagbert that the Red King turned his leopards into cats that never die. They come back in every generation to help children who will not be controlled. He says the cats hurt Manfred.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's very old, evil grandfather. He lives in the west wing of the academy and uses dark magic.

paragraphs.context: It was made by my great-grandfather, Septimus Bloor, in 1865
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Bloors' fortune comes from a false will.
paragraphs.simple: The true will of Septimus Bloor left everything to his daughter Maybelle. But Beatrice, a witch, poisoned Maybelle and made a false will. So the Bloor family got the house and treasures.

background.note: Maybelle Bloor, the daughter of Septimus Bloor (1865). A true will left everything to her, but Beatrice, a witch, poisoned her and made a false will.
Ezekiel's great-grandfather. In 1865 he made a will leaving the Bloor house and treasures to his daughter Maybelle.

paragraphs.context: We believe that Rufus gave it to Lyell Bone for safekeeping
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Bloors killed Billy's parents.
paragraphs.simple: Ezekiel says that Rufus gave a box to his friend Lyell Bone. The Bloors could not get it, so they arranged a car "accident" that killed Rufus and his wife. Their baby lived. That baby is Billy.

background.note: Rufus Raven, Billy Raven's father. He was Lyell Bone's best friend and was killed in a car 'accident' arranged by the Bloors.

paragraphs.context: This wasn’t strictly true.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Blessed the old dog understands that the strangers are bad.
paragraphs.simple: Blessed cannot understand every word, but he feels the danger. The strangers smell of the sea and wet wood. He will tell Billy, Billy will tell Cook, and Blessed hopes to get a bone.

background.note: Cook's very old, ugly, wrinkled dog at Bloor's Academy. He talks to Billy Raven.
The cook at Bloor's Academy. She is kind to the children and secretly helps Charlie and his friends.

paragraphs.context: Quickly changing the subject, Charlie explained that they were in the blue coatroom of the music students.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie explains the school's colors and rooms.
paragraphs.simple: Music students wear blue capes, drama students purple and art students green. Each group has its own coatroom and cafeteria, but they do normal lessons together.

background.note: A room where pupils keep their capes and coats. Each department has one, such as the blue coatroom.
One of the three parts of Bloor's Academy. Music students wear blue capes.

paragraphs.context: For the rest of the day Dagbert stuck to Charlie like a limpet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert will not leave Charlie alone.
paragraphs.simple: A limpet is a small sea animal that holds tight to rocks. Dagbert follows Charlie everywhere, so Charlie cannot talk to his friends. Olivia says Dagbert smells of fish.

background.note: A lively drama student at Bloor's who loves wild clothes and colored hair. She becomes one of Charlie's best friends.

paragraphs.context: Charlie would have run after the girls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is hurt by Olivia's words.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia said something unkind, and Charlie stops. He looks at her stylish clothes and was going to say she looked nice. But Dagbert said something rude first, and it seemed to come from Charlie.

paragraphs.context: At the far end of the grounds, the deep red walls of a castle could be glimpsed between the trees.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ruined Red Castle is in the school grounds.
paragraphs.simple: The Red King once lived in the castle. Charlie sometimes goes there to be safe, but it always feels uneasy because of the king's children fighting there long ago.

paragraphs.context: Furious, Charlie stormed away from Dagbert and made for the school.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie runs from Dagbert and finds Billy.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is angry. The fish smell is very strong. He goes to the blue coatroom to find Gabriel, but finds Billy Raven sitting alone instead.

background.note: An endowed music student. He can feel other people's feelings and memories by wearing their clothes. He keeps gerbils.

paragraphs.context: Charlie couldn’t concentrate.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie looks at the Red King's portrait in the King's room.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie wants to go into the painting to speak to the king, but Harken the Enchanter, a shadow behind the king, always stops him.

background.note: Dr. Bloor's son and head boy of Bloor's Academy. He is endowed: he can hypnotize people. He is cruel to Charlie.
An evil enchanter from long ago who married Lilith, the Red King's eldest daughter. He hates the Red King's family.
A round room in Bloor's Academy, with a round table and the Red King's portrait, where the endowed children do homework.

paragraphs.context: Anyway, she told me about this man,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorcas talks about Venetia's wedding plan.
paragraphs.simple: Dorcas whispers about a rich man Venetia wants to marry. Charlie hears only some words: Archie Shellhorn, poison, beads, herbs and wedding.

background.note: The youngest great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She is vain and makes dangerous enchanted clothes.
A plump, cheerful-looking endowed girl at Bloor's Academy.
A rich man, father of Eric and Miranda. Venetia Yewbeam makes him fall in love with her by magic so that he will marry her.

paragraphs.context: It was easy enough to guess the rest
paragraphs.mainIdea: Venetia used poison and magic to get a husband.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie understands: Venetia killed Archie Shellhorn's wife with poisoned beads, then put love herbs in Archie's coat. Now Archie wants to marry her.

paragraphs.context: At four o’clock Weedon unlocked the main doors
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children go home for the weekend, but Dagbert looks worried.
paragraphs.simple: At the end of the week the children rush out of school. Charlie and Billy watch from the window. Dagbert is the only one who does not look happy.

background.note: The gardener and porter at Bloor's Academy. He works for the Bloors and is not friendly to the children.
A big bedroom where many pupils sleep. Bloor's pupils sleep at school during the week.

paragraphs.context: Charlie resolved to change Cook’s mind.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie wants Cook to stay for Billy's sake.
paragraphs.simple: Cook wants to leave the school. But Billy has no family, and Cook looks after him in the holidays. The Bloors always promise to find parents for Billy, but they never do.

paragraphs.context: They crept into the kitchen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie and Billy take cookies from the kitchen.
paragraphs.simple: The boys are hungry. They eat cookies, shortbread and gingerbread in the kitchen and then go out into a yard behind it.

paragraphs.context: At the far end of the yard two people squatted in a dark corner.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys see two strange, half-animal people.
paragraphs.simple: The two figures have shining animal eyes and hair on their faces. They run up the steps on hands and feet, as fast as cats, and disappear.

paragraphs.context: At noon the boys decided to look for Cook.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys see a strange hooded figure.
paragraphs.simple: The boys are hungry and go to find Cook. In the hall they see someone in a dark cape and hood, with a strange, bent body.

paragraphs.context: There was a shriek, a flurry of paper, pins, and fabric
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dorcas is making something with magic herbs.
paragraphs.simple: The boys find Dorcas Loom. On her table are huge scissors, cans and bunches of herbs. Charlie thinks Venetia is involved.

paragraphs.context: Benjamin’s parents were already hard at work when the three boys left number twelve.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjamin's parents work as detectives.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. and Mrs. Brown are private detectives, so they often work at weekends. Today they are making new disguises. Sometimes even Benjamin does not know them.

paragraphs.context: Ingledew’s bookstore lay in Cathedral Close.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie thinks about Olivia and Emma.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie walks past the bookstore to Piminy Street. He wonders if the girls are helping Miss Ingledew, or making a plan to punish him for words he never said.

background.note: An old street behind the cathedral where the Kettle Shop stands.
Julia Ingledew, the kind owner of a bookshop near the cathedral. Uncle Paton likes her very much.
The quiet square by the cathedral where Miss Ingledew's bookshop stands, at Number Three.
Miss Ingledew's old bookshop in Cathedral Close, near the cathedral, full of rare books.

paragraphs.context: Olivia lay sprawled on Miss Ingledew’s comfy sofa.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olivia plans a game with an illusion.
paragraphs.simple: Olivia wants to make an illusion of a bird. Emma will turn into the same bird. Then Miss Ingledew must guess which bird is real.

paragraphs.context: Miss Ingledew, labeling books on the counter, looked up from her task in confusion.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Ingledew sees a strange bird in her shop.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Ingledew sees a wonderful bird and thinks it escaped from the zoo. When Emma runs in, the bird (Olivia's illusion) disappears.

paragraphs.context: The two children had moved together now.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Eric and Miranda look small and poor.
paragraphs.simple: Miranda and Eric are holding hands. Miranda's coat is too small for her. Eric's hair is long and his clothes are dirty. They are very small for their ages.

background.note: Venetia's small, quiet stepson. He is endowed: he can make stone carvings come alive and move.
Miranda Shellhorn, Archie Shellhorn's small, thin daughter. She and her brother Eric live with Great-aunt Eustacia for a while.

paragraphs.context: For his part, Paton wondered what Julia was going to think about.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton thinks about Julia and the key.
paragraphs.simple: Julia is Miss Ingledew. Paton loves her but they don't always understand each other. He plans to send the children to Venetia's house to look for a key under the troll.

background.note: Ugly, strong creatures; in the later books Count Harken uses an army of trolls.

paragraphs.context: Charlie suddenly became aware of a tall figure, just inside the window.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The shop is full of life-size statues.
paragraphs.simple: Inside the dark shop Charlie sees statues: Roman soldiers, three fierce women with clubs and axes, a man like an ogre and a knight on a horse with a lance.

paragraphs.context: Everything in Mrs. Kettle’s shop appeared to shine.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everything in the Kettle Shop is a kettle.
paragraphs.simple: The shop is full of kettles of every shape, size and color. The biggest is a copper kettle in the window, and the whole shop shines in its side.

background.note: A strong, friendly woman who runs the Kettle Shop on Piminy Street and is Cook's good friend.

paragraphs.context: He felt something to the left of him, tugging in an extraordinary way.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie feels something pull him toward an old kettle.
paragraphs.simple: As he leaves, Charlie feels a strange pull. On a dark table he sees a very old black kettle.

paragraphs.context: I hope it will never boil dry for you, Charlie,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle gives Charlie a magic kettle.
paragraphs.simple: The kettle needs no stove. It gets hot when danger is near. The hotter it gets, the more careful Charlie must be.

paragraphs.context: Charlie had noticed the kettle getting warmer.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie thinks the stone troll moved.
paragraphs.simple: The kettle is getting warm. At Venetia's house Charlie bends toward the stone troll and sees one of its eyes blink. He is sure it moved.

paragraphs.context: Charlie replaced the key and they left Darkly Wynd as quickly as possible.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie feels sorry for Eric and Miranda.
paragraphs.simple: The children leave Darkly Wynd. Charlie thinks about inviting Eric and Miranda to his house, but Eric's cold look and his interest in the kettle stop him.

background.note: The middle great-aunt, Grandma Bone's sister. She has an iron-gray bun and sometimes sees the future.
A dark, narrow alley where the three Yewbeam aunts live, at number thirteen.

paragraphs.context: The front door slammed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma Bone sees the black kettle.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tries to hide the kettle under the table, but Grandma Bone comes in and sees it at once. She always notices things Charlie wants to hide.

paragraphs.context: Maisie couldn’t stand having one of her meals interrupted in this way.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Maisie tells Grandma Bone to leave them alone.
paragraphs.simple: Grizelda is Grandma Bone's first name. Maisie bangs the chair and says the boys are cold and hungry, and the dog is doing no harm.

background.note: Charlie's other grandmother, his mother's mother. She is warm, noisy and loving, and lives with Charlie's family.

paragraphs.context: Ordinarily, Charlie would have gone to the Pets’ Café on a Sunday afternoon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie does not go to the Pets' Café today.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie does not want to see Olivia, and Tancred and Lysander are with their girlfriends. Charlie thinks the café is not a romantic place.

background.note: A tall, kind African boy in the art department. He is endowed: he can call up the spirits of his ancestors.
An endowed art student with crackling blond hair. He is a storm-bringer: his moods make wind, rain and thunder.
A café on Frog Street run by Mr. Onimous. Only people with pets are allowed in.

paragraphs.context: Indeed, it was a very cozy scene
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two animal-like faces look in through the window.
paragraphs.simple: The room is warm and comfortable. But when Charlie goes to close the curtains, he sees two faces with yellow animal eyes and hairy foreheads.

paragraphs.context: Fidelio was a great listener.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie tells Fidelio everything.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie tells Fidelio about the Kettle Shop and the attack on Uncle Paton. People say the Wilderness Wolf did it, but Paton thinks it was human. Billy says their voices are the same.

background.note: Charlie's first friend at Bloor's Academy, a music student from a big musical family. He is not endowed.

paragraphs.context: At number twelve Filbert Street, Benjamin Brown was still wide awake.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjamin goes to a meeting with his parents.
paragraphs.simple: Benjamin has had a busy weekend. His parents took him to a meeting at the town hall.

background.note: The street where Charlie lives, at number nine. Benjamin lives across the road at number twelve.
Benjamin's parents. They are private detectives and are almost always busy with their work.

paragraphs.context: Benjamin doubted it until he heard that the subject for discussion would be the Wilderness Wolf.
paragraphs.mainIdea: People at the meeting are afraid of the "wolf".
paragraphs.simple: The meeting is about the Wilderness Wolf. Benjamin learns that frightened people lie. Everyone looks and sounds afraid.

paragraphs.context: At this point Benjamin told a white lie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benjamin decides to find Asa with Runner Bean.
paragraphs.simple: A white lie is a small, harmless lie. Benjamin thinks Runner Bean can find Asa if he smells something of Asa's. He wants to do it without his parents.

background.note: Manfred's friend, a drama student with red hair and yellow eyes. He is a were-beast who changes shape at dusk.

paragraphs.context: Finding something belonging to Asa wasn’t as easy as Benjamin had hoped.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nobody knows anything about Asa's family.
paragraphs.simple: Asa's parents have never been seen. His things are all at Bloor's Academy, where Benjamin cannot go. The Bloors think Asa is a traitor because he changed sides.

paragraphs.context: By the time Benjamin got home from school the next day, the hunt was already underway.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Men go into the wilderness to hunt the "wolf".
paragraphs.simple: Half the city watches as forty men meet on the bridge. They wear all kinds of clothes and hats. Half of them carry rifles.

background.note: A wild, empty area across the river from the city, where strange things happen.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert’s crinkly hair began to unfold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert says the moon controls him.
paragraphs.simple: Dagbert says the moon controls his moods, like the tides. He cannot help being bad. If Charlie tells him about the words on the wall, he will stop following him.

paragraphs.context: It took Charlie several seconds to make sense of Dagbert’s speech.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie brings Dagbert his gold charms.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie finds seven small gold things under Dagbert's pillow: five crabs, a fish and a sea urchin. He puts them in Dagbert's glowing hands.

paragraphs.context: Drama lessons took place in the school theater.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Marlowe, the drama teacher, is described.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Marlowe writes and directs popular plays. She is small and lively, with gray and white hair, colorful shawls and long velvet skirts.

background.note: The head of the drama department at Bloor's Academy.

paragraphs.context: So sorry, Mrs. Marlowe. We do apologize.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fidelio charms Mrs. Marlowe.
paragraphs.simple: Fidelio can be very polite and charming. He says he has written a musical and asks to borrow some costumes.

paragraphs.context: Olivia flicked a switch
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children enter a dark costume room.
paragraphs.simple: A light shows rows of cupboards, leather trunks and baskets. On the other side, old stone pillars make dark spaces where nothing can be seen.

paragraphs.context: They decided not to search for the boots.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie finds a cupboard full of masks.
paragraphs.simple: The children are looking for Asa's disguise. Charlie finds a box of beards and then a cupboard of masks of every kind: animals, skulls, clowns, ghosts and monsters.

paragraphs.context: Charlie pulled on his warmest clothes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kettle is hot, which means danger.
paragraphs.simple: Before he leaves, Charlie touches the kettle. It is hot, so there is danger. He looks for the white moth, his magic wand in another shape, which protects his room.

paragraphs.context: When they had crossed the bridge, the three children walked down the path
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children go into the wilderness.
paragraphs.simple: The children follow the hunters' path. Olivia's big flashlight helps them through the thick plants into the forest, where they find a narrow path.

paragraphs.context: The woman began to shake.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Pike tells how her husband was shot.
paragraphs.simple: The strange woman is Asa's mother. Her husband was shot while trying to lead the hunters away from their son. She hid his body under branches.

paragraphs.context: They decided not to return by the stone bridge.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children choose the dangerous iron bridge.
paragraphs.simple: The stone bridge will be busy, so they use the iron bridge. They hope to reach the Pets' Café before anyone sees Mrs. Pike.

paragraphs.context: Easy it certainly wasn’t.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is very hard to carry Mrs. Pike.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Pike keeps fainting and falling into their arms. When they reach the bridge, the children are very tired, but their troubles are only starting.

background.note: Asa Pike's mother, a sad woman who worries about her son.

paragraphs.context: The bridge suddenly tilted violently.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bridge tips, and someone falls.
paragraphs.simple: Runner Bean crawls toward them. The bridge tips and everyone slides. Olivia holds a railing and Mrs. Pike's feet, but past Olivia the bridge is empty.

paragraphs.context: Standing at the very end of Frog Street, the Pets’ Café had an ancient look about it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pets' Café is very old.
paragraphs.simple: The café is built into the old city wall. Its sign shows whiskers, paws, tails and wings. You cannot go in without a pet.

background.note: A narrow old street behind the cathedral where the Pets' Café is.

paragraphs.context: The Onimouses’ cozy kitchen never failed to lift Charlie’s spirits.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three Flame cats sleep in the café kitchen.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie always feels happier in this kitchen. The Flame cats, yellow, orange and copper, are asleep on a cupboard.

background.note: Three magic copper-colored cats, Aries, Leo and Sagittarius, who protect Charlie and the good endowed children.

paragraphs.context: Words poured out of Mrs. Pike
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Pike tells the story of the Merromals.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Pike says that Cafall the Changer, a son of the Red King, left the castle and sailed to a far land. Its people are the Merromals, people who can change like her.

background.note: A strange people from a faraway land. Mrs. Pike says she is a Merromal.
Asa Pike's father, a Merromal. Hunters shoot him in the wilderness.
Cafall the Changer, one of the Red King's sons. He could change shape. He sailed away and found the land of the Merromals.

paragraphs.context: We brought our son to this kingdom fifteen years ago.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Merromals love books.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Pike explains that the Merromals are well educated. Cafall took his father's book of legends, and since then they have collected many books.

paragraphs.context: It was that man Weedon who caught poor Asa.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Bloors want a box in exchange for Asa.
paragraphs.simple: Weedon caught Asa and locked him up. The Bloors told his parents to find a box with mother-of-pearl in Charlie's old house. "No box, no boy."

paragraphs.context: Not a sign of it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lyell Bone hid the box.
paragraphs.simple: The box is not in the house. Ezekiel says Lyell hid it. Under the spell Lyell forgot, but now the Bloors are afraid he will remember.

paragraphs.context: The small man spread his hands.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Onimous goes back to his café.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Onimous says anything is possible in this city. He tells Mrs. Pike to stay and hurries out with dog biscuits and bird seed.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Pike had been listening to them all with a frown
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Pike is sure the Bloors want her dead.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Pike failed to find the box and knows its secret. She thinks the Bloors made the bridge tip to drown her, not the children.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Pike couldn’t be consoled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Pike fears for Asa.
paragraphs.simple: She thinks the Bloors will try to make Asa evil again because he is a changer. Runner Bean is afraid of her.

paragraphs.context: The Pets’ Café was remarkably busy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The café is full of animals.
paragraphs.simple: The children must jump over cats and rabbits, squeeze past a big dog and a tiny pony, and bend under a flying owl.

paragraphs.context: Not that I think it’s a story,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lauren cannot believe the story.
paragraphs.simple: Lauren is not endowed. She thinks the Bloor's children are interesting, but a "not-quite-human" person in the kitchen is hard to believe.

background.note: Lysander's friendly girlfriend. She is not endowed and does not go to Bloor's Academy.

paragraphs.context: It was decided that they should all meet up again the following afternoon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The friends plan to meet again.
paragraphs.simple: Lysander will try to bring Tancred, but Tancred does not want to leave his girlfriend Tracy, who does not like animals.

background.note: Tancred's girlfriend in cb06. She does not like animals.

paragraphs.context: Miss Ingledew regarded her empty glass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Ingledew tells the history of Piminy Street.
paragraphs.simple: Piminy Street is the oldest street. Magicians like Feromel the blacksmith and Melmott the stonemason lived there. They usually fought, but they worked together to stop the great fire.

background.note: Mrs. Kettle's ancestor, a blacksmith and magician who made a magic kettle long ago.
A stone mason and magician who lived in Piminy Street long ago. His stone statues can come to life.

paragraphs.context: A narrow alley ran between the backyards of the houses
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girls see gray forms in a yard.
paragraphs.simple: From the window the girls look at a dark alley with trash and weeds. In one small yard there are gray shapes that make strange shadows.

paragraphs.context: You must hold the window open as wide as you can.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma turns into a bird.
paragraphs.simple: Emma stands high on the bed. She imagines black wings and the night sky, and then she feels real wings lifting her up.

paragraphs.context: Taking another breath, this time for courage as much as anything
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma sees someone working in a hot room.
paragraphs.simple: Emma lands on a window sill. Inside she sees a tall person in a metal helmet, blue work clothes and leather gloves. It is a woman.

paragraphs.context: Emma perched on a streetlight and surveyed the row of ancient houses.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma flies along Piminy Street and sees something strange.
paragraphs.simple: The street feels full of magic. Emma looks through a window above the fish shop and sees underwater colors on the wall and someone with a shining face on the bed.

paragraphs.context: She had seen more than enough for one night.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Emma is shocked by something.
paragraphs.simple: Emma has seen enough. She does not want to see more magic. She flies up but is so surprised that she almost falls.

paragraphs.context: As I almost said, Charlie’s father comes out of a trance
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton thinks Lyell was punished because of the box.
paragraphs.simple: Paton thought Ezekiel put Lyell under a spell for revenge. Now he thinks Lyell was punished because he knew about the box and would not give it up.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert looked past them at a sewer grate in the road.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert attacks the girls with water.
paragraphs.simple: Dagbert makes water burst out of a drain. It follows the girls like a snake and almost pulls them down.

background.note: Mrs. Kettle's shop on Piminy Street, which sells kettles. Its door knocker is a little bronze kettle.

paragraphs.context: Come in then, both of you.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle helps the wet girls.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Kettle takes the girls to a warm room and tells them to take off their wet clothes. She goes to get dry ones.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Kettle’s features softened.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle has Feromel's skills.
paragraphs.simple: She makes tools and iron things but does not usually use magic. She was very happy when someone asked her to make a special sword.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Kettle put up her hand.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A knight asked for the sword.
paragraphs.simple: A silent knight came at night, in chain mail and a helmet with red feathers. His face was hidden.

paragraphs.context: As they jogged up to Darkly Wynd
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie keeps the sword a secret from Benjamin.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie is still carrying the heavy kettle. He tells Benjamin about Dagbert, but not about the sword, because Benjamin is not endowed.

paragraphs.context: Charlie raced after him, with Chattypatra wriggling and squealing under his arm.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys run through Darkly Wynd with Chattypatra.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie carries the noisy dog Chattypatra. Nobody opens a window, because the people in Darkly Wynd do not want to know what happens there.

background.note: Venetia Yewbeam's small, noisy dog. Charlie and Benjamin take her away when they rescue her.

paragraphs.context: Charlie took the mug of tea and sniffed it suspiciously.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lysander and Gabriel arrive.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie gets a flower tea. Lysander comes with Gabriel. Tancred stayed with his girlfriend; Lauren is visiting her grandmother.

paragraphs.context: Could there be any doubt?
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red King's cloak may be in the wrong hands.
paragraphs.simple: Guanhamara took the cloak to Italy, and it came down to Gabriel's family. Gabriel once wore it and was not hurt by Harken's attack.

background.note: A daughter of the Red King who fled his castle and married an Italian prince. She tried to cure the deadly boa.

paragraphs.context: In a chest under my parents’ bed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cloak has disappeared.
paragraphs.simple: Gabriel can feel the feelings of people whose clothes he wears, but the cloak comforts him. When he asked his father for it, his father said it was gone.

paragraphs.context: For the first time Charlie wondered if the knight on the bridge had been trying to save them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Is the Red Knight good or bad?
paragraphs.simple: Charlie wonders if the knight on the bridge was trying to help. But maybe he stole the cloak and will use the magic sword against them.

paragraphs.context: Where it was — the passage under the castle.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Onimous remembers a secret passage.
paragraphs.simple: His great-grandmother found a trapdoor behind the school stage. An old man told her a passage goes deep down, and long ago it went all the way to the river.

background.note: Orvil Onimous, a small furry-looking man who runs the Pets' Café and does pest control with the Flame cats.

paragraphs.context: Manfred knew that the Flame cats were responsible for his dreadful injuries
paragraphs.mainIdea: Manfred wants to punish Charlie and keep Asa.
paragraphs.simple: The Flame cats hurt Manfred while protecting Charlie, so Manfred blames Charlie. He wants Asa to stay in the dark until he becomes a wild beast again.

paragraphs.context: Charlie put his hand against the wall and, to his horror, found it sliding away beneath his fingers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is pulled down into a dark alley.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua's magnetism and the twins' power pull Charlie down the moving steps. He is thrown onto cold stone. His legs are heavy and he cannot even cry out.

paragraphs.context: The stone never reached him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A strong wind saves Charlie.
paragraphs.simple: A sudden wind throws the falling stone away and carries Joshua and the twins up the alley.

background.note: A strange new boy with paper stuck in his hair. He is endowed with magnetism: things and people are drawn to him.
Telekinetic twin girls at Bloor's Academy, relatives of Zelda Dobinski. They can move things with their minds.

paragraphs.context: When Charlie finally summoned up the courage to lift his head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie sees someone kind.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie looks up slowly, afraid of another attack. He sees blue jeans, a navy jacket and a smiling face with spiky blond hair: Tancred.

paragraphs.context: The thunderstorm had sent almost all the citizens indoors.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children go home from the café.
paragraphs.simple: The children think Charlie went home, so they leave. Mr. Onimous gives Runner Bean beef treats and Chattypatra ice cream.

paragraphs.context: He landed on straw piled at the back of a room.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is in the past with a huge man.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie travels through the old kettle into the past. He lands in a room with a full moon in the window. A very big, strong man is feeding a fire: Feromel the blacksmith.

paragraphs.context: The stone people didn’t appear to see him.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie cannot save Feromel.
paragraphs.simple: Stone statues are attacking Feromel. Charlie tries to help, but the stone man throws him across the room.

paragraphs.context: Don’t look so downcast, my dear.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle comforts Charlie.
paragraphs.simple: She says Charlie could not change the past. She thinks the old kettle shows how her ancestor Feromel died, and she wonders why.

paragraphs.context: The boys had no choice but to help her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They move the big stove.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie, Tancred and Mrs. Kettle pull the stove from the wall so they can see into the chimney.

paragraphs.context: Then we’ll make it bigger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Kettle breaks the chimney with a hammer.
paragraphs.simple: She pushes the stove with her bottom and swings a big hammer at the chimney.

paragraphs.context: Charlie removed the right glove and laid it on the stove.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie finds a loose brick.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie feels the chimney wall. One brick moves, but he thinks about the stolen cloak: should a thief get a magic sword?

background.note: A mysterious knight in a red cloak and a silver helmet with red feathers, who comes to help Charlie.

paragraphs.context: Charlie put his right hand into the cavity.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie finds the hidden sword hilt.
paragraphs.simple: He pulls out something wrapped in red cloth and gives it to Mrs. Kettle. His heart is racing.

paragraphs.context: He watched Mr. Weedon lock and bolt the heavy doors
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy is lonely at school.
paragraphs.simple: Billy stays at school for the weekend and soon regrets it. He hopes Cook can bring Rembrandt to him.

background.note: A black rat. First Mr. Boldova's pet, later Billy Raven's. He can talk to Billy.

paragraphs.context: Billy knocked. There was no reply.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy looks into a tidy room.
paragraphs.simple: Billy looks into a room with a tidy bed, a chair, drawers and a cupboard. The slippers look new.

paragraphs.context: As Billy trudged up one of the many staircases
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy remembers Ezekiel's false promises.
paragraphs.simple: Ezekiel used to give Billy cocoa and promise new parents if he helped him. The parents never came.

paragraphs.context: Wait a minute, then.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook follows Blessed.
paragraphs.simple: Cook puts on her bathrobe and follows Blessed. She feels something bad is happening at the school.

paragraphs.context: There were two ways of entering Cook’s secret apartment.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook goes through her secret way.
paragraphs.simple: Cook unlocks a small door and pushes a cupboard to get into a corridor. She is too big for the dog flap.

paragraphs.context: Blessed set off at a trot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook is afraid near the attics.
paragraphs.simple: Blessed walks slowly because he is old. Near the attics Cook is afraid that Lord Grimwald will come out at her.

paragraphs.context: Keep your voice down.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Uncle Paton has found Bartholomew to help.
paragraphs.simple: The Browns found Bartholomew Bloor. He will wait with his van near the stone bridge until dawn.

paragraphs.context: Julia and I have been doing some research
paragraphs.mainIdea: The secret passage goes to the river.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Paton says the passage from the school ends in some trees above the river path. The Bloors may know about it.

paragraphs.context: So I’ve got nothing to worry about, then.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Joshua and the twins are hurt.
paragraphs.simple: Joshua has a black eye and the twins are hurt. Joshua points at Charlie and the other children stare.

paragraphs.context: All over the city.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie is not sure where Asa is.
paragraphs.simple: Manfred knows Charlie wants to rescue Asa, but not when. Charlie is only guessing from what Mr. Onimous said.

paragraphs.context: Olivia’s sharp voice brought Charlie back to earth.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Olivia will make fake vans.
paragraphs.simple: Charlie asks Olivia to make illusions of small white vans like Bartholomew's, to confuse anyone who follows.

paragraphs.context: Charlie opened the first trunk.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie and Billy find clothes for Asa.
paragraphs.simple: In the costume room they take a coat, a beret, green trousers and brown boots for Asa.

paragraphs.context: With light from both the candle and the moth
paragraphs.mainIdea: The white moth calms the beast.
paragraphs.simple: The moth flies around the beast and covers its legs with light. The beast stops growling.

paragraphs.context: They began to move again, slowly and painfully
paragraphs.mainIdea: Water fills the tunnel.
paragraphs.simple: The water reaches their waists. Charlie is afraid the river will sweep them away when they come out.

paragraphs.context: Far above the tunnel, Tancred Torsson was making his way across the grounds
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tancred finds Dagbert making the flood.
paragraphs.simple: Tancred can feel water. He knows Charlie is in trouble and finds Dagbert smiling under a tree, making the water rise.

background.note: The Red King's castle from long ago. Its red tower and broken walls still stand outside the city.

paragraphs.context: They were now walking up a steep incline.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children get out of the tunnel.
paragraphs.simple: They see the moon and climb out into some trees beside the path. Everything is bright in the moonlight.

paragraphs.context: There was a mighty crack and the lance broke in two
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Red Knight fights the stone knight.
paragraphs.simple: The Red Knight's sword cuts the stone knight in half, and the stone horse falls into the river.

paragraphs.context: Raising his arms, Lysander spun around the room
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lysander calls his ancestors.
paragraphs.simple: Lysander chants and drums sound. Ghostly tall men with gold armbands and spears appear between the pillars, and Manfred backs away.

paragraphs.context: Dagbert Endless lay in bed, his face covered in scratches.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dagbert holds something gold.
paragraphs.simple: Dagbert is hurt and talks about the wind. He holds gold in his fist.

paragraphs.context: Old Ezekiel wheeled himself to Manfred’s door and knocked.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ezekiel thinks his plan worked.
paragraphs.simple: Ezekiel asks Manfred if Asa is gone, Charlie finished and Billy gone too. There is no answer.

paragraphs.context: Cook gave Charlie an extra-large portion
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cook gives the children a good breakfast.
paragraphs.simple: Cook bought eggs herself because the children deserve a good breakfast.

paragraphs.context: There was an exotic-looking stamp on the back and his father’s handwriting.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Charlie gets a postcard from his father.
paragraphs.simple: His father writes about the trip and promises to take Charlie next time to see the whales.

paragraphs.context: But she chats so much. You know, barks and growls
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dog's name puts Cleopatra and chat together, because the dog makes a lot of sound.
paragraphs.simple: Miranda says the dog was first called Cleopatra. The dog barks and growls all the time, so their mom named her Chattypatra. That name puts chat together with Cleopatra. Miranda stops, looks at Eric, who is close to tears, and then she goes on.

paragraphs.context: a voice that kept repeating, “Dog ahoy! Dog ahoy!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: A bird shouts a ship hello, but it says the hello to a dog.
paragraphs.simple: Dogs are barking in the cafe. Then people hear shouts, a horse sound, and a voice that keeps saying Dog ahoy. Ahoy is a hello from a ship, so the bird is saying hello to the dog.

paragraphs.context: The cross was in the form of two winged leopards
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bar across the handle looks like two big cats with wings.
paragraphs.simple: Feromel says the others will not get what they want. He opens a red cloth and shows a bright handle for a long blade. The gold part has birds with red jewel eyes, in a diamond shape. The bar across the handle looks like two big cats with wings and blue spots.

sentences.context: Through his father, he is descended from the Red King and through his mother, from Mathonwy, a Welsh magician and friend of the Red King.
sentences.simple: His father's family goes back to the Red King, and his mother's family goes back to Mathonwy.
sentences.main: He is descended from the Red King and from Mathonwy.

parts.text: Through his father,
parts.meaning: On his father's side,

parts.text: he is descended from the Red King
parts.meaning: the Red King is his ancestor

parts.text: and through his mother,
parts.meaning: and on his mother's side,

parts.text: from Mathonwy,
parts.job: The verb "is descended" is not repeated.
parts.meaning: he comes from Mathonwy,

parts.text: a Welsh magician and friend of the Red King.
parts.meaning: a magician from Wales who was the Red King's friend.
